newsitem.title: USA: Infamous drug helps relieve AIDS patients' mouth sores.
newsitem.headline: Infamous drug helps relieve AIDS patients' mouth sores.

text.p: The drug thalidomide, notorious for causing birth defects when it was given to pregnant women in the 1950s, can alleviate painful mouth and throat sores in those infected with the AIDS virus, according to a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
"Thalidomide is clearly effective in treating this condition," said a group of researchers led by Dr. Jeffrey Jacobson of the Bronx Veterans Affairs Medical Centre in New York City.

In a double-blind, four-week study, 29 volunteers were given thalidomide while another 28 received placebos. Jacobson and his colleagues found the drug completely healed the sores in 55 percent of the thalidomide recipients, compared to 7 percent among those taking the placebo once a day.
The thalidomide produced some troublesome side effects: seven of the 29 reported feeling excessively sleepy, seven developed a rash and six stopped treatment because of toxicity.
Perhaps more importantly, thalidomide, which is manufactured by several companies, increased the amount of AIDS virus circulating in the blood, which often means the deadly infection is progressing.
As a result, "we urge caution in using thalidomide in HIV-infected persons after the two to four weeks of short-term treatment," Jacobson cautioned.
But AIDS-infected patients may be willing to take the risk because the large ulcer-like mouth sores are extremely painful and can interfere with eating.
Even when the thalidomide did not completely heal the ulcers in four weeks, the area of soreness had decreased by more than 50 percent in all but 10 percent of the volunteers.
The thalidomide recipients gained an average of 4 pounds (1.8 kg) during the treatment because they could eat easily again; the placebo recipients showed no weight gain.

A single dose of thalidomide can lead to birth defects if given to a pregnant woman, so women of child-bearing age infected with the AIDS virus who chose to take thalidomide should be warned of the special risks, researchers said.
Foetuses exposed to thalidomide have severely shortened arms and legs. The side effects led to the drug being banned in the United States.
But recent research has suggested that it can be a useful treatment in other conditions besides mouth sores.
A 1992 study found evidence that it can help prevent rejection following a bone marrow transplant. Thalidomide is also being studied as a possible treatment for some forms of leprosy.
The American Medical Association Encyclopaedia of Medicine said thalidomide was used as a sleeping drug, but was never approved by the Food and Drug Administration for sale in the United States.
